summary.text: Lesson 3-4 covers polynomial long division and synthetic division, and the two theorems that come with them: the Remainder Theorem (dividing by x − a leaves P(a)) and the Factor Theorem (it is a factor exactly when P(a) = 0).

why.text: Division is how a polynomial gets broken down, and the Factor Theorem is the doorway into finding roots — which is what the next two lessons are entirely about. Getting fluent here pays off twice.

objectives.text: Divide polynomials by long division and, where the divisor is linear, by synthetic division
Write an answer as quotient plus remainder over divisor
Apply the Remainder Theorem to find a remainder by substitution
Apply the Factor Theorem to test whether a linear expression is a factor

parentNote.text: Two mechanical traps account for most lost marks here, and both are in the questions. The first is the SIGN: dividing by (x + 5) means synthetic-dividing with −5, because you use the value that makes the divisor zero — solving "divisor = 0" rather than copying the sign is the habit that fixes it. The second is MISSING TERMS: x³ − 7 needs the row 1, 0, 0, −7, and leaving the zeros out silently shifts every coefficient into the wrong column, producing a confident wrong answer with nothing visibly broken. Predicting the quotient’s degree first (dividend minus divisor) catches that one every time.

nextUp.text: Do a couple of divisions both ways — synthetically and by substituting — so the two agree.

cards.def:
**Splitting a polynomial into a quotient and a remainder, exactly like long division with numbers.**
• dividend ÷ divisor = quotient + remainder⁄divisor.
• 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 2 works the same way as a polynomial division — the shape of the answer is identical.
cards.hint: Same shape as number division: a whole part and a leftover.

cards.def:
**Works for ANY divisor, of any degree.**
• Divide the leading terms, multiply back, subtract, bring down, repeat.
• The subtraction step is where signs get lost — you are subtracting the whole product, not just its first term.
cards.hint: Divide, multiply, subtract, bring down. The subtraction is the dangerous step.

cards.def:
**A shortcut that works ONLY when the divisor is linear, of the form x − a.**
• Much faster than long division, but it is not general.
• For a divisor like x² + 1 or 2x − 3, you need long division instead.
cards.hint: Linear divisors only. Anything else is long division.

cards.def:
**Dividing by (x − 2) means you synthetic-divide with +2.**
• The number you use is the value that makes the divisor ZERO, so the sign flips.
• Dividing by (x + 5) means using −5, since x + 5 = 0 at x = −5.
cards.hint: Use the number that makes the divisor equal zero — not the one you see written.

cards.def:
**Every missing power needs a 0 in the coefficient row.**
• x³ − 7 is really x³ + 0x² + 0x − 7, so its row is 1, 0, 0, −7.
• Leaving a gap out shifts every later coefficient into the wrong column and makes the whole division wrong.
cards.hint: Write the polynomial in standard form with nothing missing before you start.

cards.def:
**The bottom row of a synthetic division gives the quotient’s coefficients, and the very last number is the remainder.**
• The quotient starts one degree LOWER than the dividend.
• A remainder of 0 means the divisor divided evenly — it is a factor.
cards.hint: Last number is the leftover; everything before it is the answer.

cards.def:
**deg(quotient) = deg(dividend) − deg(divisor).**
• A cubic divided by a linear gives a quadratic.
• Checking this before you start tells you how many coefficients the answer should have — a free check on your work.
cards.eq: deg q = deg P − deg d
cards.hint: Subtract the degrees to predict the shape of the answer.

cards.def:
**Dividing P(x) by (x − a) leaves a remainder of exactly P(a).**
• So you can find a remainder by SUBSTITUTING, with no division at all.
• To find the remainder when P is divided by (x − 3), just compute P(3).
cards.hint: The remainder is just the function evaluated at the number that zeroes the divisor.

cards.def:
**(x − a) is a factor of P(x) exactly when P(a) = 0.**
• It is the Remainder Theorem with remainder zero — no leftover means it divided evenly.
• This is the bridge to finding roots, which is what Lessons 3-5 and 3-6 are built on.
cards.hint: Zero remainder and "is a factor" are the same statement.

cards.def:
**Quotient plus remainder over divisor — the remainder never just gets dropped.**
• (x² + 4x + 14) + 19⁄(x − 2) is a complete answer; the quotient alone is not.
• Only when the remainder is 0 does the quotient stand by itself.
cards.hint: A leftover has to appear in the answer, written over the divisor.
Bring down, multiply, add — and the last add gives the remainder.

cards.def:
**The remainder of (2x³ + x − 5) ÷ (x − 2) is 13, found by substituting.**
• P(2) = 2(8) + 2 − 5 = 16 + 2 − 5 = 13.
• No division was done at all — that is the Remainder Theorem earning its keep.
cards.hint: If a question asks only for the remainder, substitute rather than divide.

questions.q: To divide a polynomial by (x − 6) using synthetic division, which number do you use?
questions.hint: You use the value that makes the divisor zero.
steps: Set the divisor equal to zero: x − 6 = 0.
Solving gives x = 6.
That is the number synthetic division uses.
So you use 6.

ex.main: **6.** The sign flips from the one written, because the number you need is the ZERO of the divisor. The habit that prevents the error is actually solving x − 6 = 0 rather than copying the sign you see.
ex.tip: Same rule for (x + 6): it is zero at −6, so you would use −6.

questions.q: When is synthetic division allowed?
opts: Only when the divisor is linear, of the form x − a
Only when the remainder will be zero
Only when the dividend has degree 3 or less
questions.hint: Think about what the shortcut’s single row of numbers can represent.
steps: Synthetic division compresses the divisor down to one number.
That only works when the divisor is x minus a constant.
A divisor like x² + 1, or 2x − 3, cannot be reduced to one number this way.
So it is linear divisors of the form x − a only.

ex.main: **Only when the divisor is linear, of the form x − a.** The dividend can be any degree at all, and the remainder can be anything — those are not restrictions. The restriction is entirely on the DIVISOR, which is why long division still has to exist.
ex.tip: When the divisor is anything else, long division is the tool. It always works.

questions.q: Writing 2x⁴ − 3x + 1 as a row of coefficients for synthetic division gives
questions.hint: Every power from the highest down to the constant needs a slot.
steps: The degree is 4, so there are five slots: x⁴, x³, x², x, constant.
x⁴ has coefficient 2.
x³ and x² are missing, so both are 0.
Then −3 for x and 1 for the constant: 2, 0, 0, −3, 1.

ex.main: **2, 0, 0, −3, 1.** A degree-4 polynomial always needs exactly five coefficients. Writing only the terms you can see shifts everything into the wrong column and the whole division comes out wrong — with no obvious sign that anything went astray.
ex.tip: Count the slots first: degree + 1. If your row is shorter, a placeholder is missing.

questions.q: What does the Remainder Theorem say?
opts: The remainder equals the leading coefficient of P(x)
Dividing P(x) by (x − a) always leaves a remainder of zero
The remainder is always smaller than the divisor
Dividing P(x) by (x − a) leaves a remainder of P(a)
questions.hint: It connects dividing to substituting.
steps: The theorem links the remainder to the function’s value.
Specifically, the remainder of P(x) ÷ (x − a) is P(a).
That lets you find a remainder by substituting instead of dividing.
So: dividing P(x) by (x − a) leaves P(a).

ex.main: **Dividing P(x) by (x − a) leaves a remainder of P(a).** A remainder of zero is the special case — that is the Factor Theorem, and it is what makes (x − a) a factor. The theorem’s real value is that it replaces a whole division with one substitution.
ex.tip: Remainder Theorem: any remainder. Factor Theorem: the remainder is zero.

questions.q: A degree-5 polynomial is divided by a degree-2 polynomial. What degree is the quotient?
questions.hint: Degrees subtract on division, the way they add on multiplication.
steps: Multiplying adds degrees, so dividing subtracts them.
deg(quotient) = deg(dividend) − deg(divisor).
That is 5 − 2 = 3.
The quotient has degree 3.

ex.main: **3.** Degrees subtract on division for the same reason they add on multiplication — quotient times divisor has to rebuild the dividend, and 3 + 2 = 5. Knowing the answer’s degree in advance tells you how many coefficients to expect, which catches a dropped placeholder.
ex.tip: Predict the degree first; then a quotient with the wrong number of terms announces itself.

questions.q: A synthetic division ends with a last number of 0. What does that mean?
opts: The polynomial itself is equal to zero everywhere
The divisor is a factor of the polynomial
A mistake was made somewhere in the working
The quotient has to come out as zero as well
questions.hint: The last number of the bottom row is the remainder.
steps: The final number is the remainder.
A remainder of 0 means the division came out evenly.
Dividing evenly is exactly what "is a factor" means.
So the divisor is a factor of the polynomial.

ex.main: **The divisor is a factor.** This is the Factor Theorem showing up in the arithmetic. It says nothing about the polynomial itself being zero — P(x) is zero only at that one x-value, not everywhere — and the quotient is certainly not zero.
ex.tip: Zero remainder is good news: you have found a factor and can keep factoring the quotient.

questions.q: Divide x³ + 4x² − 7x − 10 by (x − 2).
questions.hint: Use +2, and take the row as 1, 4, −7, −10.
steps: Bring down 1. Multiply 1 · 2 = 2; add to 4 to get 6.
Multiply 6 · 2 = 12; add to −7 to get 5.
Multiply 5 · 2 = 10; add to −10 to get 0.
Bottom row 1, 6, 5, 0: the quotient is x² + 6x + 5 with remainder 0.

ex.main: **x² + 6x + 5, remainder 0.** The quotient drops one degree from the dividend, as it must. The zero remainder means (x − 2) is a factor — and since x² + 6x + 5 factors further into (x + 1)(x + 5), the whole cubic is (x − 2)(x + 1)(x + 5).
ex.tip: A zero remainder is an invitation to keep factoring the quotient.

questions.q: Use the Remainder Theorem: what is the remainder when x³ − 4x² + x + 6 is divided by (x − 3)?
questions.hint: Substitute the value that makes the divisor zero — no division needed.
steps: The divisor is zero at x = 3, so compute P(3).
The remainder is 0.

ex.main: **0.** One substitution replaces the whole division. And the zero is informative: it means (x − 3) is a factor of this cubic, which is the Factor Theorem arriving for free.
ex.tip: When a question asks only for the remainder, substituting is always faster than dividing.

questions.q: What is the remainder when x⁴ − 3x² + 2x − 1 is divided by (x + 1)?
questions.hint: Careful with the sign of the value you substitute.
steps: x + 1 = 0 gives x = −1, so compute P(−1).
2(−1) = −2, and the constant is −1.

ex.main: **−5.** The divisor (x + 1) is zero at −1, not +1 — substituting +1 instead gives −1, which is offered as a wrong option precisely because it is what the sign slip produces. Note (−1)⁴ is positive while 2(−1) is negative; even and odd powers behave differently.
ex.tip: Solve divisor = 0 rather than reading the sign off the bracket.

questions.q: Which division requires LONG division rather than synthetic division?
questions.hint: Check the DIVISOR in each, not the dividend.
steps: Synthetic division needs a divisor of the form x − a.
(x − 4), (x + 2) and (x − 2) are all that shape.
(x² + 3) is degree 2, so it cannot be reduced to a single number.
That one needs long division.

ex.main: **(x³ + 2x − 1) ÷ (x² + 3).** Only the divisor decides. The dividends here range from degree 3 to degree 5 and none of that matters — a degree-5 dividend with a linear divisor is still perfectly fine for synthetic division.
ex.tip: Look only at what you are dividing BY. The thing being divided is never the constraint.

questions.q: Divide 2x³ − 3x² + 4 by (x + 1).
questions.hint: There is a missing term — write the row carefully — and the divisor is zero at −1.
steps: The x term is missing, so the row is 2, −3, 0, 4.

ex.main: **2x² − 5x + 5, remainder −1.** Two traps in one question: the missing x term needs a 0 placeholder, and the divisor (x + 1) is zero at −1. Checking with the Remainder Theorem confirms it — P(−1) = −2 − 3 + 4 = −1.
ex.tip: You can always check a synthetic division’s remainder independently by substituting. Two methods agreeing is real confidence.

questions.q: A student divides x³ + 2x − 5 by (x − 1) and writes the row as 1, 2, −5. What will go wrong?
opts: The coefficients belong in ascending order, lowest power first
Nothing is wrong — the row lists every coefficient there is
The divisor sign is wrong: (x − 1) should be entered as −1
The x² placeholder is missing, so every column shifts over by one
questions.hint: Count the slots a degree-3 polynomial needs.
steps: A cubic needs four coefficients: x³, x², x, constant.
x³ + 2x − 5 has no x² term, so that slot is 0.
The correct row is 1, 0, 2, −5.
Writing only three numbers shifts the 2 and the −5 left, so the division is wrong throughout.

ex.main: **The x² placeholder is missing, so every column shifts over by one.** A degree-3 dividend always needs four coefficients, and the answer will come out as a quadratic-looking thing that is simply wrong — with nothing obviously broken to alert her. Predicting the quotient’s degree first is the check that catches it.
ex.tip: Degree + 1 slots, always. A short row is a missing placeholder every time.

questions.q: For P(x) = x³ + x² − 10x + 8, which of these is a factor?
questions.hint: The Factor Theorem turns this into four quick substitutions.
steps: (x − a) is a factor exactly when P(a) = 0.
P(2) = 8 + 4 − 20 + 8 = 0. That one works.

ex.main: **(x − 2).** Testing candidates by substitution is far faster than dividing by each one. And the sign matters: (x − 2) asks about P(2), while (x + 2) asks about P(−2) — which here is 24, nowhere near zero.
ex.tip: This is exactly the tool Lesson 3-6 builds on to find all the roots of a polynomial.

questions.q: P(x) divided by (x − 4) gives a quotient of x² + 3x − 1 and a remainder of 6. What is P(x)?
questions.hint: Reverse the division: multiply the quotient by the divisor and add the remainder.
steps: Division says P(x) = divisor × quotient + remainder.
Combine: x³ − x² − 13x + 4.
Add the remainder 6: x³ − x² − 13x + 10.

ex.main: **x³ − x² − 13x + 10.** The relationship runs both ways, and reversing it is the standard way to CHECK a division. Forgetting to add the remainder gives x³ − x² − 13x + 4 — offered here because it is the near-miss that catches most people.
ex.tip: Check any division by multiplying back and adding the remainder. It should rebuild the dividend exactly.

questions.q: For what value of k is (x + 2) a factor of x³ − 2x² + x + k?
questions.hint: Use the Factor Theorem and solve for k.
steps: (x + 2) is a factor exactly when P(−2) = 0.
That is −18 + k, and it must equal 0.
So k = 18.

ex.main: **18.** Substituting x = −2 gives −8 − 8 − 2 + k = −18 + k, and setting that to zero gives k = 18. Using +2 by mistake would give k = −2, and dropping the lone x term would give 16 — both offered here, because both are what the two usual slips actually produce.
ex.tip: The Factor Theorem turns "make this a factor" into a plain equation in k.

questions.q: Divide x³ − 8 by (x − 2).
questions.hint: Two missing terms — build the coefficient row before anything else.
steps: x³ − 8 is x³ + 0x² + 0x − 8, so the row is 1, 0, 0, −8.
Use +2. Bring down 1; 1 · 2 = 2, and 0 + 2 = 2.
4 · 2 = 8, and −8 + 8 = 0. So x² + 2x + 4, remainder 0.

ex.main: **x² + 2x + 4, remainder 0.** Both placeholder zeros were needed. The zero remainder is no accident — x³ − 8 is a difference of cubes, and Lesson 3-3’s identity gives exactly (x − 2)(x² + 2x + 4). Division and factoring agreeing is a real check on both.
ex.tip: When a division comes out even, look for the identity that predicted it.

questions.q: What is the remainder when 3x³ − 2x² + 5 is divided by (x − 1)?
questions.hint: Substitute rather than divide.
steps: The divisor is zero at x = 1, so compute P(1).
The x term is absent and the constant is 5.

ex.main: **6.** Substituting 1 is about as fast as this gets — every power of 1 is 1, so the remainder is just the sum of the coefficients. That shortcut works for any division by (x − 1) and is worth remembering on its own.
ex.tip: Divide by (x − 1) and the remainder is always the coefficients added up.

questions.q: Which statement about a remainder of 0 is TRUE?
opts: The polynomial has no roots at all, of any kind
The divisor is a factor, so the polynomial factors further
The quotient must come out as 0 as well, for the same reason
The division was done incorrectly and should be worked again
questions.hint: A remainder of zero is the Factor Theorem speaking.
steps: A zero remainder means the divisor divided evenly.
Dividing evenly is what being a factor means.
So P(x) = (divisor)(quotient), and the quotient may factor further still.
The divisor is a factor and factoring can continue.

ex.main: **The divisor is a factor, so the polynomial factors further.** It is the opposite of a problem — a zero remainder is progress, because it has split the polynomial into two pieces and the quotient is now a smaller problem to attack.
ex.tip: Every zero remainder reduces the degree of what is left to factor.

questions.q: Divide x⁴ − 3x² + 1 by (x² − 2). What is the quotient?
questions.hint: The divisor is not linear, so synthetic division is out — and predict the quotient’s degree first.
steps: deg 4 − deg 2 = 2, so the quotient is a quadratic.
x⁴ ÷ x² = x². Multiply back: x⁴ − 2x². Subtract: −x² + 1.
−x² ÷ x² = −1. Multiply back: −x² + 2. Subtract: −1.
So the quotient is x² − 1 with remainder −1.

ex.main: **x² − 1.** A quadratic divisor rules synthetic division out entirely — this one has to be long division. Predicting the quotient’s degree as 2 first is what tells you the answer is a quadratic, so an option with an x term in it can be ruled out before any arithmetic.
ex.tip: Degree subtraction predicts the SHAPE of the answer, which narrows the options before you start.

questions.q: You find that P(2) = 0 for P(x) = x³ + 2x² − 5x − 6. What is the most useful next step?
opts: Substitute more values one by one until another gives zero
Conclude that 2 must therefore be the only root it has
Divide P(x) by (x + 2) and factor whatever is left over
Divide P(x) by (x − 2) and factor the quadratic that comes out
questions.hint: A known root gives you a known factor — use it to shrink the problem.
steps: P(2) = 0 means (x − 2) is a factor, by the Factor Theorem.
Dividing by it turns the cubic into a quadratic, which is far easier to handle.
Here the quotient is x² + 4x + 3, which factors as (x + 1)(x + 3).
So P(x) = (x − 2)(x + 1)(x + 3), and all three roots fall out at once.

ex.main: **Divide by (x − 2) and factor the quotient.** One known root converts a cubic into a quadratic, and a quadratic can be finished by factoring or the Quadratic Formula — no more guessing needed. Note the sign: P(2) = 0 gives the factor (x − 2), not (x + 2). Hunting for more roots by substitution would work eventually but throws away the shortcut you have just earned.
ex.tip: This is the whole method of Lesson 3-6: find one root, divide it out, finish the smaller polynomial.
